TITLE: Investigating Non-Asymptotic Sample Complexity Bounds for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We propose a new concentration inequality for the least-squares solution in the constrained regression problem used in KernelSHAP. We assume that the value functions v(S) are bounded by a constant M, and the kernel weights k(S) are sampled according to the correct distribution. We then show that the expected squared error of the KernelSHAP solution is bounded by the term O((d-1)/\eps^2 \cdot (d \log(d) / n)^(d-2)), where \eps is the tolerance parameter, d is the dimension of the problem, and n is the number of sampled subsets. This bound can be used to obtain a non-asymptotic sample complexity guarantee for KernelSHAP.
CONTROLS: We provide a baseline bound by directly analyzing the least-squares solution using Dudley's inequality, and we also include ablations to study the effects of varying the tolerance parameter \eps and the Sampling without Replacement.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: We expect this proposal to provide a valuable first step towards understanding the sample complexity of KernelSHAP, and may shed light on the relative performance of KernelSHAP versus LeverageSHAP. However, the bound may be tight in some cases, making it difficult to obtain sample-efficient estimators.

TITLE: Comparing KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP on Real-world Datasets
PROPOSAL: We conduct an experimental study on the performance of KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP on a range of real-world datasets, including those used in previous work on Shapley value estimation. We compare the accuracy of the two estimators using metrics such as mean absolute error and mean squared error, and also investigate the running times and sample complexities of the two methods.
CONTROLS: We use six real-world datasets from the SHAP library, including Adult, COMPAS, and Diabetes. For each dataset, we evaluate the performance of KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP with different tolerance parameters and sampling rates. We also include ablations to compare the performance of KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP when sampling with and without replacement.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: We expect this proposal to provide valuable insights into the relative performance of KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, and may help identify when to use each algorithm. However, the experimental results may depend on the specific datasets and hyperparameters used, and may not generalize to all settings.

TITLE: Understanding the Effect of Sampling Distributions on Shapley Value Estimation
PROPOSAL: We investigate how different sampling distributions used in randomized Shapley value estimators, such as KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, affect the accuracy and sample complexity of the estimators. We consider a range of sampling distributions, including the original KernelSHAP distribution, LeverageSHAP, and two new distributions that we propose. We analyze the theoretical properties of the estimators under each distribution, and also conduct experiments on real-world datasets to evaluate their performance.
CONTROLS: We will include baseline results for the original KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP distributions, as well as results for our proposed new distributions. We will also attempt to identify scenarios in which one distribution is superior to another.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect this proposal to provide valuable insights into the design of sampling distributions for Shapley value estimators, and may lead to improvements in the accuracy and sample efficiency of the estimators. However, evaluating the performance of the estimators under each distribution may require significant computational resources.

TITLE: Improved Concentration Inequalities for Least-Squares Solutions
PROPOSAL: We strengthen the concentration inequality we proposed in our initial proposal by providing a new exponential concentration inequality that more accurately captures the behavior of the least-squares solution in the constrained regression problem used in KernelSHAP. We assume that the value functions v(S) are sub-Gaussian with a bounded variance, and show that the expected squared error of the KernelSHAP solution is bounded by the term O((d-1)/\eps^2 \cdot (d \log(d) / n)^{d/2}), which has a better dependence on d than our original bound. This improved bound can be used to obtain a more accurate non-asymptotic sample complexity guarantee for KernelSHAP.
CONTROLS: We include a comparison to our original bound, as well as a comparison to the baseline bound using Dudley's inequality. We also ablate different assumptions about the value functions v(S) to understand the robustness of the improved bound.
COST: 830.4
PREDICTION: We expect this revised proposal to provide a substantial improvement in the accuracy of our sample complexity guarantee for KernelSHAP, and may lead to improved performance on large datasets. However, the assumptions about the value functions v(S) may be restrictive in some cases.

TITLE: A Fast and Provably Accurate Method for Computing Shapley Values on Large Datasets
PROPOSAL: We propose a new method for computing Shapley values that is fast, accurate, and provably efficient. Our method is based on using a combination of leverage scores and random sampling to select a subset of data points that is representative of the entire dataset. We provide a theoretical analysis of the accuracy and efficiency of our method, and also conduct experiments on large datasets to evaluate its performance.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to existing methods for computing Shapley values, including KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP. We also ablate different parameters of our method to understand its robustness and flexibility.

However, the theoretical guarantees of our method may be sensitive to specific parameters and assumptions.

TITLE: Investigating the Role of Temporally Grounded Transformers for Change Description
PROPOSAL: 
We will evaluate a Temporally Grounded Transformer (TGT) model variant, specifically designed for temporal change description, where the transformer encoder is pre-trained on a chronological alignment of density-map representations of satellite images. This setup will be applied to the popularانگ Districts dataset, which offers a large-scale, real-world benchmark for change description. Performance will be evaluated using the standard metrics of BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR for natural-language description. In addition, an ablation study will investigate the importance of different components of the model, such as the use of temporally groundedinformation, the number of transformer layers, and the type of cross-attention mechanism used.
CONTROLS: 
A baseline model without temporally grounded information, a random initialization baseline, and a general-purpose MLLM pre-trained on a large corpus of text data.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: 
The TGT model should outperform the baseline model and the random initialization baseline on both BLEU and METEOR scores, demonstrating its ability toreason about change in a temporal context. However, it may struggle with fine-grained changes, particularly if they are sparse and occur over long periods, which could lead to decreased performance on the METEOR score.

TITLE: Evaluating Temporally Consistent Future Forecasting using Temporal Change Description
PROPOSAL: 
We will investigate the effectiveness of a Temporal Change Description (TCD) model in informing temporally consistent future forecasting. Specifically, we will use the pre-trained TGT model from Proposal 1 to generate a natural-language description of the expected changes occurring in the next time step. This description will then be used as text guidance to condition a state-of-the-art diffusione-based image generator (e.g., DDPM) to synthesize the future image. The performance of this setup will be compared to the baseline of using DDPM alone, as well as an ablation study investigating the importance of the TCD model's description for temporal consistency. The Land Use Land Cover Change (LULCC) dataset will be used to evaluate the performance of this setup.
CONTROLS: 
The baseline model using DDPM alone, and an ablation study removing the TGT model's description from the text guidance.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: 
The temporally consistent future forecasting setup should outperform the baseline model in terms of both visual quality metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM) and temporal consistency metrics (e.g., mean absolute difference between generated and ground-truth changes).

PROPOSAL:

Specifically, we will create four variants of the LULCC dataset by randomly downsampling the original dataset by 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. We will then evaluate the performance of the TGT model on each of these variants, using the standard metrics of BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR for natural-language description. PROPOSAL:

Specifically, we will divide the input sequence into overlapping sub-sequences, and use a separate TGT model to capture temporal relationships within each sub-sequence. The output from each sub-sequence will then be used as input to the next sub-sequence, allowing the model to build a hierarchical representation of temporal relationships. TITLE:  Multi-Step Forecasting with Adaptive Attention 
PROPOSAL: We develop an online forecasting method, dubbed OAA-TS (Online Attention Adaptation for Time Series), that leverages an attention mechanism to selectively focus on the most relevant information for multi-step forecasting. At each time step, OAA-TS automatically updates its attention weights based on a small batch of recent samples, allowing it to adapt to concept drift and novel patterns. To mitigate the delayed feedback issue, we use a combination of the current forecast and the ground truth values available so far to compute a partial loss function at each intermediate step. We evaluate OAA-TS on the M4 dataset for multi-step forecasting in various domains, including traffic flow forecasting and electricity consumption forecasting.
CONTROLS: A baseline using DCRNN with an adapter module for comparison with state-of-the-art methods, and an ablation study removing the attention mechanism to show its effectiveness.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Compared to DCRNN, OAA-TS will show a significant reduction in multi-step forecasting error, especially indomains where concept drift is frequent. However, the method may struggle with extremely long predictions (e.g., more than 10 steps ahead), where the delayed feedback issue becomes more pronounced.

TITLE:  Emphasizing Long-Term Dependencies with Hierarchical Learning 
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new online learning framework, dubbed HOLTS (Hierarchical Online Learning for Time Series), which exploits hierarchical dependencies in time series data to improve forecasting accuracy, especially for long-term predictions. HOLTS consists of two main components: a top-down hierarchical layer that models long-term trends and seasonality, and a bottom-up hierarchical layer that captures short-term fluctuations. At each time step, the model updates the top-down layer using a small batch of recent samples and then adjusts the bottom-up layer based on the updated long-term trends. We anticipate that HOLTS will outperform existing methods for long-term forecasting, such as OAA-TS, particularly in domains like weather forecasting.
CONTROLS: Compare HOLTS to OAA-TS and other strong baseline methods like BART, and ablate the top-down and bottom-up components to demonstrate their individual contributions.
COST: 280
PREDICTION: HOLTS will show a substantial improvement in accuracy for long-term predictions (e.g., more than 5 steps ahead) compared to state-of-the-art methods, but might be less effective in domains where short-term variations are more significant.

PROPOSAL: We develop a novel online learning approach, called FOMM (Fading Memory Mechanism for Multi- Step Forecasting), that effectively handles distribution shift and novel patterns in time series data. FOMM uses a fading memory mechanism to weigh the contributions of historical data, giving less emphasis to older observations and more emphasis to recent ones. This approach enables the model to adapt quickly to changing patterns while retaining knowledge of long-term trends. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we evaluate FOMM on various real-world time series forecasting benchmarks, including the M4 dataset.

However, FOMM might require more computational resources due to the necessity of recalculating the fading memory weights at each time step.

TITLE:  Offline-Online Model Transfer for Time Series Forecasting 
PROPOSAL: We propose an offline-online model transfer approach, dubbed OMOT (Offline-Online Model Transfer), that leverages a pre-trained offline forecasting model to initialize an online forecasting model. By fine-tuning the pre-trained model on a small batch of online data, OMOT can adapt the model to the changing environment and distribution, while also leveraging the prior knowledge and representations learned from the offline training data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of OMOT on various real-world time series forecasting benchmarks.

However, the method may require careful selection of the offline training data to avoid performance degradation due to domain shift or concept drift.

TITLE: Adversarial Constrained Policy Optimization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a robust adversary model that captures the worst-case behavior of proxy rewards consistent with the assumed correlation constraint. Assume the adversary can be modeled as a reward function that equals the proxy reward in states visited by the reference policy and is arbitrary otherwise. To guarantee robustness, optimize a policy that minimizes an upper bound on the true reward achievable by this adversary. This upper bound is obtained by maximizing the adversary's reward over the states not visited by the reference policy, given the correlation constraint. The resulting problem can be solved using a novel constrained optimization formulation, which incorporates the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure as a constraint. By executing the optimized policy, we can provide a lower bound on its true performance and establish a guarantee on its robustness against the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint.

PREDICTION: This approach should improve robustness guarantees, but may incur higher optimization cost and conservatism compared to ORPO. The guarantee may be too pessimistic in cases where the actual worst-case proxy reward is significantly better or worse than the assumed correlation level, leading to suboptimal policy performance in practice.

PROPOSAL: We introduce kernel-induced equivariant metanetworks, a novel approach that captures functional equivalence classes of neural network parameters through kernel methods.
